concept: Projectile range from launch angle and launch speed
sourceSummary: A projectile launched from level ground travels a range set by the square of its launch speed and the sine of twice its launch angle.

stages.challenge: The angle is fixed at 30°. Land the ball 50 meters away.
stages.teaches: Launch speed alone, with the angle held still.

lock.note: Launch angle is fixed for this challenge

hints: Only the speed can move. Fire once and see which way you missed.
Range grows with the square of speed, so small speed changes matter more than they look.
At 30° you need a launch speed of about 24 m/s.
stages.debriefing: Doubling the speed would have quadrupled the range. Speed enters the range equation squared, which is why the ball overshot so quickly once you pushed it.

stages.challenge: Now the speed is fixed at 20 m/s. Land the ball 35 meters away.
stages.teaches: Launch angle alone, with the speed held still.

lock.note: Launch speed is fixed for this challenge

hints: Only the angle can move this time. Try a low angle and a high one.
Range peaks at 45° and falls away evenly on either side.
Both 30° and 60° land in the same spot. Try each.
stages.debriefing: Two different angles reach the same range, one low and fast across, one high and slow. Angles that add up to 90° always land together, because sin(2θ) is symmetric around 45°.

stages.challenge: Both controls are unlocked. Land the ball 80 meters away, then find a second way.
stages.teaches: Angle and speed trading off against each other.
hints: A launch closer to 45° needs less speed to go the same distance.
Find one answer, then move the angle 15° away from 45° and see how much speed you have to add.
45° at 28 m/s works. So does 30° at 30 m/s.
stages.debriefing: Many pairs of angle and speed land at 80 meters. The closer you launch to 45°, the less speed you need, because 45° splits the speed most evenly between staying up and moving forward.

completion: You isolated speed, then angle, then traded them against each other. Speed counts twice because it is squared. Angle counts through sin(2θ), which peaks at 45° and pairs every low launch with a high one.
subject: Physics
